subject: Judith
note: Evidence for Judith's figure page. Every quotation is in judith.quotes.json and passes verify-quotes.mjs. Fetched texts are in design/saints-hub/sources/people/judith/ (gitignored). Judith is not in the BSB: her lines quote the World English Bible (US edition with the deuterocanon, the quiz's own translation; the shared file matches ebible.org/eng-web, not eng-webbe, which spells 'saviour'), copied to web-judith.txt. Capitals for God are applied on the page. The few other Bible lines (Judges 4:9, 5:24, Esther 4:16, 1 Samuel 25:3, Luke 1:42) are BSB.

life.text: Her husband Manasses died of the heat at the barley harvest; she was a widow three years and four months; she lived in a tent on her roof, wore sackcloth and fasted except on Sabbaths, new moons and feasts; she was beautiful and rich; no one spoke evil of her.
Daughter of Merari; her genealogy runs through fifteen names back to Israel; of the tribe of Simeon ('God of my father Simeon'); Manasses was of her tribe and family.
life.source: Judith 8:1-2; 9:2 (WEB). Encyclopaedia Britannica (1911), R. H. Charles: 'a beautiful and pious widow of the tribe of Simeon'. Catholic Encyclopedia (1910): 'Why carry out the genealogy of a fictitious person through fifteen generations?'

life.text: The army at the siege: 170,000 foot soldiers and 12,000 horsemen; Holofernes seized the springs; after 34 days the water ran out; women and young men fainted in the streets; the people demanded surrender; Ozias asked for five more days.
life.note: Holofernes' first muster was 120,000 foot and 12,000 mounted archers (2:15); 7:2 gives 170,000 for the march on Bethulia. The page uses 7:2, the siege itself.

life.text: She sent her maid for the rulers, rebuked them for testing God, and promised a deed that would 'go down to all generations', without saying what.

She prayed face down with ashes on her head at the hour of the evening incense in Jerusalem; she recalled Simeon's sword; she asked God to bless the deceit of her lips and to break the enemy 'by the hand of a woman'.

She dressed in the 'garments of gladness' she wore while her husband lived; her maid carried wine, oil, roasted grain, figs and bread; the elders were astonished; the men watched until they could see her no more.

Taken by the Assyrian watch, she claimed to be fleeing; a hundred men escorted her; she told Holofernes her people would sin by eating the first fruits and tithes, and that she would pray nightly and tell him when; he promised 'your God will be my God'.
She refused his food, ate her own, and for three days went out each night to the spring in the valley to wash and pray; on the fourth day came the banquet.

At the banquet Holofernes drank more than on any day of his life; Bagoas shut the tent; she took his sword from the bedpost, took his hair, prayed, struck twice and cut off his head; the maid put it in the food bag; they left as if to pray.

At the gate she showed the head and the canopy; she swore he had not defiled her; the head was hung on the wall; at sunrise the men sallied; Bagoas found the body; the army fled, pursued past Damascus; the camp was plundered for thirty days.

Joakim the high priest and the elders blessed her; she led the women's dance crowned with olive; she sang her song; at Jerusalem she dedicated Holofernes' goods and canopy to God; she stayed three months while the people feasted.

She never remarried; she grew old in her husband's house to 105; set her maid free; died in Bethulia; was buried in Manasses' cave; Israel mourned seven days; she distributed her goods to both families; no one troubled Israel in her days or long after.
Her name means 'Jewess'. Bethulia cannot be identified.
life.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica (1911), R. H. Charles: 'Judith ... i.e. [Yehudit], Jewess'; 'Bethulia (Betylua) and Betomestham ... (neither place can be identified)'. Catholic Encyclopedia (1910): 'the names, Judith (Jewess), Achior (brother of light), and Bethulia ... sound rather like symbolic names'; 'no trace of the existence of such a place is to be found (unless we accept the theory of Conder)'.

life.text: She appears in chapter 8; the last nine of the book's sixteen chapters are about her.
life.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica (1911): 'to whom the last nine of its sixteen chapters relate'.

fathers.text: Clement of Rome retells her story (1 Clement 55), with Esther beside her.

Ambrose: 'she went out to die ... she went but out to fight'; 'her purity unspotted' (Duties 3.13); 'holy Judith' and 'not so much a work of her hands, as much more a trophy of her wisdom' (Concerning Widows 7).

Jerome's preface: the Jews count it among the apocrypha; written in 'Chaldean' (Old Aramaic); he translated it because the Nicene Council was said to count it Scripture; 'a single night's work'; 'Receive the widow Judith, example of chastity'.
fathers.source: Jerome, Preface to Judith, tr. Andrew S. Jacobs (2004), released to the public domain by the translator; Latin from PL 29:37-39 on the same page.
fathers.note: NPNF2 6 has no preface to Judith. The Jacobs text has footnote numbers inline; no quotation on the page spans one.

fathers.text: Sulpicius Severus (Sacred History 2.14-16) dates her under Ochus, and notes the book's Nebuchadnezzar 'was certainly not the one who took Jerusalem'. Augustine (City of God 18.26) places her story between Cyrus and Darius and says the Jews are said not to have received it into the canon.
Origen: 'Tobias (as also Judith), we ought to notice, the Jews do not use. They are not even found in the Hebrew Apocrypha, as I learned from the Jews themselves.'
fathers.source: Origen, Letter to Africanus, chapter 13 (EB1911 gives the chapter), tr. Frederick Crombie, ANF 4.

book.text: Catholic and Orthodox Old Testaments hold it: Carthage 419, canon 24 ('Tobit. Judith. Esther.' among 'the Canonical Scriptures'); Trent, session 4 (1546), 'Tobias, Judith, Esther'; the Confession of Dositheus (Synod of Jerusalem, 1672), question 3, names 'Judith' among books it calls 'genuine parts of Scripture'.
book.source: NPNF2 14, tr. Henry Percival (newadvent 3816); Trent, tr. J. Waterworth 1848 (Hanover Historical Texts); Dositheus, tr. J. Robertson 1899 (crivoice.org, which makes no copyright claim on the text).

book.text: Protestant canon excludes it; the English Apocrypha places it after Tobit; the Thirty-Nine Articles, Article 6, list 'The Book of Judith' among books the Church reads 'for example of life and instruction of manners' but not to establish doctrine ('as Hierome saith').
book.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (1910): 'does not exist in the Hebrew Bible, and is consequently excluded from the Protestant Canon'. EB1911: 'in the English Apocrypha it is placed between Tobit and the apocryphal additions to Esther'. Book of Common Prayer, Oxford (Henry Frowde), about 1900, archive.org compray00chur: Article 6 read in the scan (verify-quotes kind 'scan'); the 1885 American 'Book Annexed' (cu31924029458167) has the same words.
book.note: The brief asked for a public-domain BCP. justus.anglican.org refused the fetch (403) and bcponline.org had no Articles page; the Oxford printing of about 1900 is public domain in the US.

book.text: Historicity, both sides: CE 1910 (Hugh Pope): 'Catholics with very few exceptions accept the book of Judith as a narrative of facts, not as an allegory'; 'The Fathers have ever looked upon the book as historical'; admits 'very serious difficulties' (Nebuchadnezzar never king of Nineveh; Bethulia unknown; symbolic names); conservative answers (the husband's death, the geography of the passes, the genealogy). EB1911 (R. H. Charles): 'The book in its fuller form was most probably written in the 2nd century B.C. The writer places his romance two centuries earlier'.
book.source: Catholic Encyclopedia, 'Book of Judith'; Encyclopaedia Britannica 1911, 'Judith, The Book of' (Wikisource, rendered text via the API).

feasts.text: Orthodox: the OCA lists 'Righteous Judith' on the Sunday of the Forefathers (the Sunday between 11 and 17 December; 14 December in 2025), with the one line 'Information about the Righteous Judith may be found in the Old Testament book bearing her name.'
feasts.source: OCA, lives of the saints, 14 December 2025, entry 606; the Sunday of the Forefathers entry 80 gives the 11 to 17 December rule. Russian Wikipedia (lead only) adds that the Orthodox honour her as a foremother on that Sunday, citing Dionysius of Fourna's Painter's Manual.
feasts.note: The OCA does not list her on the Sunday before the Nativity (checked the 21 December 2025 listing). No fixed day, so the page has no feasts panel; the saint section carries it.

feasts.text: West: no day. Not in the 1916 Roman Martyrology, the 1969 Calendarium, the USCCB 2026 calendar, the Church of England calendar, the Episcopal Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022 (her book is only read there, on other days), the LCMS or the ELCA calendars.
feasts.source: grep of the shared calendar files for 'Judith'.

feasts.text: The Church of England's Common Worship: Daily Prayer includes Canticle 45, 'A Song of Judith'.
feasts.source: Church of England, Canticles (Daily Prayer) page (fetched), and the canticle list on the calendar page (shared/cofe-calendar.txt).

pictures.text: Band: Judith, August Riedel, 1840, oil on canvas 131 x 96 cm, Neue Pinakothek, Munich (Wikidata Q21451900). Commons licence tag {{PD-art|PD-old-100-expired}}. Original 2478 x 3418; cropped to the top 78% (0 to 2666 px) so that Holofernes' head, at the lower left edge of the painting, is not in the file; saved 1673 x 1800, 328 KB. posM 50% 12%, posD 50% 16% (eyes at 27% of the crop: about a third down on a 390 x 335 phone crop and on a 625 x 450 panel).
Card: 480 x 600 cut from the Riedel original (x 615 to 1815, y 142 to 1642): face centred, eyes at about 38% from the top.

Portrait: The Return of Judith to Bethulia, Sandro Botticelli, about 1470, tempera on panel 31 x 24 cm, Uffizi (Wikidata Q2267509). Commons licence tag {{PD-Art|PD-old-100-expired}} (the photograph is from Flickr user hen-magonza, covered by PD-Art). Original 3627 x 4928; detail x 38% to 97%, y 0 to 56% (Judith with the sword and olive branch; her maid is cut to a raised arm at the left edge, and the head she carries is outside the crop); saved 1163 x 1500, 336 KB.

Gallery (wide screens only): Judith, Benjamin-Constant, possibly about 1886, oil on canvas 120.7 x 80 cm, The Metropolitan Museum of Art, 59.185, gift of J. E. Gombos, 1959. Commons permission {{Cc-zero}} (Met Open Access). Original 2450 x 3722; saved whole at 987 x 1500, 246 KB. No head, no blood: she holds a sheathed sword.

Looked at and not used: Artemisia Gentileschi's Pitti Judith and her Maidservant (the head in the basket is plain to see), Cristofano Allori (she holds the head), Giorgione (foot on the head, small face), Vincenzo Catena and Fede Galizia (the head on show). Botticelli's whole panel was set aside as the portrait because Judith's face is small in it.

could_not_verify: The 2004 Roman Martyrology (not public): the page says only that the 1916 edition and today's General Roman Calendar have no day for her.
The Catholic Liturgy of the Hours' use of her canticle at Morning Prayer (a lead from Russian Wikipedia): not fetched, left off.
The medieval Jewish link between Judith and Hanukkah (a Wikipedia lead): no public-domain source fetched in reasonable time, left off.
Luther's preface calling the book a spiritual poem: no public-domain English text fetched; the page names no Reformer.
Who first confused Judith with Jael: not claimed; the myth is framed as the difference between the two stories.

checked: Every quotation: verify-quotes exits 0 (69 printed, 65 entries).

Numbers against the WEB: 170,000 foot and 12,000 horse (7:2), five days (7:30), three nights at the spring (12:7), the feast on the fourth day (12:10), 105 (16:23); 34 days (7:20); three years and four months (8:4).
Augustine, City of God 18.26 ('During the same time', the time of Cyrus); the Catholic Encyclopedia's fifteen generations; Charles in the 1911 Britannica; the Met's date 'possibly ca. 1886'.
Her book: each side in its own words; our voice states only that Nebuchadnezzar ruled from Babylon after Nineveh fell, which is history, not a verdict on the book.
Pictures: Commons licence tags read by API (Riedel PD-art, Botticelli PD-Art, Benjamin-Constant Cc-zero); band shows no head or blood; card face centred.
changed: Fact 'In art': it said 'as in Botticelli's picture on this page', but the page's Botticelli detail crops out the head and most of the maid. Now: 'Nearly always with a sword, as in all three pictures on this page. Often her maid is with her, carrying the head of Holofernes.'
Gallery caption: 'Judith in the tent' had no source (the Met calls it only 'Judith'); now 'Judith with a sheathed sword'.
Italics: *Thirty-Nine Articles* in 'Among the Apocrypha, or left out', as Mary's page does.
